items.q: Peak velocity is 2.0 m per s across a stenotic valve. What is the peak gradient by 4 times velocity squared?
items.exp: Bernoulli reads 4 times 2.0 squared equals about 16 mmHg, so the gradient follows velocity squared. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Bernoulli gradients.

items.q: Peak velocity is 2.5 m per s across a stenotic valve. What is the peak gradient by 4 times velocity squared?
items.exp: Bernoulli reads 4 times 2.5 squared equals about 25 mmHg, so the gradient follows velocity squared. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Bernoulli gradients.

items.q: Peak velocity is 3.0 m per s across a stenotic valve. What is the peak gradient by 4 times velocity squared?
items.exp: Bernoulli reads 4 times 3.0 squared equals about 36 mmHg, so the gradient follows velocity squared. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Bernoulli gradients.

items.q: Peak velocity is 3.5 m per s across a stenotic valve. What is the peak gradient by 4 times velocity squared?
items.exp: Bernoulli reads 4 times 3.5 squared equals about 49 mmHg, so the gradient follows velocity squared. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Bernoulli gradients.

items.exp: Bernoulli reads 4 times 4.0 squared equals about 64 mmHg, so the gradient follows velocity squared. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Bernoulli gradients.

items.q: Peak velocity is 4.5 m per s across a stenotic valve. What is the peak gradient by 4 times velocity squared?
items.exp: Bernoulli reads 4 times 4.5 squared equals about 81 mmHg, so the gradient follows velocity squared. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Bernoulli gradients.

items.q: Why may the net gradient be lower than 4 times velocity squared in mild obstruction?
o: A brisk proximal velocity above 1 m per s must be subtracted
items.exp: The full equation keeps proximal kinetic energy, so ignoring a fast proximal jet overreads the net drop. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on extended Bernoulli.

items.q: What is the key strength of continuous wave Doppler?
o: It records very high velocities but not their depth
items.exp: Continuous wave listens along the whole line, so high jets are caught at the cost of range detail. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on continuous wave principles.

items.q: What is the key strength of pulsed wave Doppler?
items.exp: Pulsed wave ranges gates by timing, so velocity at one exact site is read cleanly within its limit. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on pulsed wave principles.

items.q: The pulsed wave trace wraps around the baseline at high velocity. What is this?
items.exp: Pulsed sampling cannot track beyond half the pulse rate, so the peak folds over the scale. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Nyquist limit and aliasing.

items.q: Aliasing obscures a high velocity jet on pulsed wave. Which move keeps the same probe position?
o: Raise the scale with higher pulse repetition and shift the baseline
items.exp: A higher pulse rate lifts the Nyquist ceiling and baseline shift adds display room, so the true peak unfolds. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on correcting aliasing.

items.q: Deeper sampling worsens aliasing on pulsed wave. Why?
o: Round trip time forces a lower pulse rate
items.exp: Sound takes longer to return from depth, so pulses go out slower and the velocity ceiling falls. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on depth and pulse rate.

items.q: On colour Doppler, red and blue mean what by convention?
o: Red toward and blue away from the probe
items.exp: Colour maps direction along the beam, so red approaches while blue recedes under the standard map. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on colour direction convention.

items.q: A mosaic of bright mixed colours appears at a valve. What does it mean?
o: High velocity disturbed flow with aliasing
items.exp: Jets beyond the colour scale fold into mixed hues, so mosaic marks fast turbulent flow needing spectral study. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on colour aliasing.

items.q: Colour fills outside the vessel walls. What knob is too high?
items.exp: Excess colour gain paints noise over tissue, so turning gain down until speckle just clears is the fix. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on colour gain.

items.q: Low velocity tissue signal clutters the flow trace. Which control removes it?
items.exp: The wall filter drops slow strong wall motion while keeping faster blood signal on screen. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on wall filter.

items.q: The Doppler beam meets flow at 60 degrees. What is the error?
o: Velocity reads half the true value
items.exp: The machine reads the cosine component, and cosine of 60 is one half, so the display halves the truth. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on angle dependence.

items.q: What beam to flow angle keeps error small for gradients?
items.exp: Cosine near zero angle stays near one, so aligning below 20 degrees keeps underreading tiny. Guideline: ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on spectral Doppler technique.

items.q: Why must gradients be taken from the window with the highest velocity?
o: Any angle error only underreads, so the peak is truest
items.exp: Underreading only lowers values, so the highest clean signal from several windows sits closest to truth. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on multi window interrogation.

items.q: Aortic stenosis jet is best recorded from which window choice?
o: The window giving the highest velocity, often apex or right parasternal
items.exp: Jet direction varies, so the window most parallel to flow gives the peak and others may underread badly. Guideline: ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on aortic stenosis Doppler.

items.q: Continuous wave shape in severe aortic stenosis looks like what?
o: Dense late peaking jet with a slow rise
items.exp: Fixed obstruction holds pressure through systole, so the dense jet peaks late with a rounded rise. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on stenotic jet shapes.

items.q: Mitral regurgitation jet from anterior leaflet disease points where?
o: Backward into the atrium away from the diseased leaflet
items.exp: The jet hugs the opposite wall by Coanda effect, so anterior disease throws a posterior jet. Guideline: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on jet direction.

items.q: Tachycardia raises the mean gradient across a stenotic mitral valve. Why?
o: Short diastole forces the same flow through less time
items.exp: Less diastolic time means higher flow per second, and gradient follows flow squared across a fixed hole. Guideline: ASE and EACVI 2017 stenosis guideline, section on heart rate effects.

items.q: Pressure half time of the aortic regurgitation jet is steep and short. What does it mean?
items.exp: A big hole lets aortic and ventricular pressures meet quickly, so the slope steepens and half time shortens. Guideline: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on pressure half time.

items.q: Dense holosystolic mitral regurgitation signal with a full envelope means what?
o: Large regurgitant flow through the whole of systole
items.exp: Brightness tracks red cell numbers and the full envelope spans systole, so density plus timing marks a big leak. Guideline: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on spectral signs.

items.q: Tissue Doppler e prime is sampled where?
o: At the mitral annulus septal and lateral points
items.exp: Annular motion tracks relaxation, so septal and lateral annular sites give the e prime pair. Guideline: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function guideline, section on annular velocities.

items.q: A larger pulsed wave sample volume widens the spectrum. Why?
o: More velocities across the gate are averaged together
items.exp: A wide gate mixes slow edge and fast core flow, so the trace broadens with many speeds at once. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on sample volume size.

items.q: High pulse repetition frequency mode helps when pulsed wave aliases. What does it do?
o: Adds extra sample gates to lift the velocity ceiling
items.exp: Extra gates sample faster than depth alone allows, so high velocities unfold at some cost in range certainty. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on high pulse repetition frequency.

items.q: Pulmonary vein systolic flow reverses in severe mitral regurgitation. Why?
o: The regurgitant wave floods the atrium in systole
items.exp: A large systolic leak pressurises the atrium above vein pressure, so vein flow turns backward in systole. Guideline: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on supporting signs.

items.q: Diastolic mitral inflow is recorded with pulsed wave at which site?
o: At the leaflet tips in the four chamber view
items.exp: Tips mark the narrowest inflow where E and A separate cleanly, so the gate sits there with a small volume. Guideline: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function guideline, section on inflow recording.

items.q: Aortic regurgitation jet is best seen in which colour view?
o: Parasternal long axis with the jet below the valve in diastole
items.exp: The long axis cut lines the outflow with the valve, so the diastolic jet origin and length show clearly. Guideline: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on jet imaging.

items.q: Why is continuous wave used for the peak tricuspid velocity rather than pulsed wave?
o: The jet often exceeds the pulsed limit
items.exp: Regurgitant jets run several metres per second, beyond pulsed range, so continuous wave captures the peak. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on choosing continuous wave.

items.q: Spectral gain is set too high. What does the trace show?
o: Bloomed thick edges with filled noise
items.exp: Excess gain paints noise into the envelope, so edges bloom and weak signals look falsely strong. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on spectral gain.

items.q: What does the Nyquist limit equal on pulsed Doppler?
items.exp: Sampling theory caps clean tracking at half the pulse rate, so faster flow folds at that ceiling. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on Nyquist limit.

items.q: Colour scale is set very low. What false picture appears?
o: Widespread mosaic suggesting fast flow everywhere
items.exp: A low ceiling folds even normal flow, so mosaic spreads and jets look larger than truth. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on colour scale.

items.q: Why does lowering transmit frequency reduce aliasing?
o: Lower frequency shifts the same velocity lower on the scale
It raises the pulse rate directly
items.exp: Doppler shift scales with frequency, so the same speed folds less at lower frequency with more penetration. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on frequency and aliasing.

items.q: Mitral inflow velocities shift with loading. Why do grades use several signs?
o: One number alone misleads when preload changes
items.exp: Filling velocities follow load, so E over e prime with volume and velocity together grades fairly. Guideline: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function guideline, section on loading effects.

items.q: Aortic outflow VTI is 30 cm with a normal valve. What does a high VTI alone prove?
o: High stroke flow, not obstruction by itself
items.exp: VTI tracks volume per beat, so a tall outflow VTI with normal velocity means high output rather than a narrow valve. Guideline: ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on outflow Doppler.

items.q: Diastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta lasts the whole of diastole. What grade of leak fits?
items.exp: Runoff through all of diastole needs a large hole, so holodiastolic reversal marks severe regurgitation. Guideline: ASE 2017 valvular regurgitation guideline, section on descending aorta flow.

items.q: Stenotic jet velocity is recorded at 60 degrees to flow. What must be done before grading?
o: Realign below 20 degrees from another window
items.exp: A 60 degree angle halves the reading, so only a well aligned peak can grade severity. Guideline: ASE Doppler and flow assessment guidance within the ASE 2019 TTE guideline, section on angle dependence.
